tagline: Rolling sand ridges and former railway tracks shape a Florida drive.
intro: The Green Mountain Scenic Byway winds through rolling hills near Lake Apopka, passing along Sugarloaf Mountain’s eastern side. Florida designated it on July 19, 2004. The Florida Scenic Highways program highlights its small towns and recreation, and describes the hills as a draw for cyclists who come to train, tour and compete. Sugarloaf is the peninsula’s highest ground at 312 feet, a ridge of rounded peaks above flatter land. The road offers views across this landscape, while the West Orange Trail shares the byway corridor through downtown Winter Garden.

The corridor’s recreational routes follow earlier working landscapes. At Sugarloaf, citrus replaced grape growing by the 1940s; freezes devastated groves in the 1980s, and land was rezoned for housing as the industry faded. Between Oakland and Winter Garden, two railroads once ran beside each other. The West Orange Trail now uses both rights-of-way, continuing through Winter Garden in Plant Street’s median where trains once ran.

For this southbound stretch, start at Howey Cross Roads and travel through Ferndale and Montverde toward Oakland. Montverde occupies Lake Apopka’s southwest shore. Continue through Oakland and Tildenville toward Winter Garden, where the trail runs down the center of the byway through downtown.
notice: In Winter Garden, the trail follows the former railroad through Plant Street’s median.

moments.title: Sugarloaf Mountain
moments.text: Sugarloaf rises to 312 feet, the highest point on the Florida peninsula, though Britton Hill in the Panhandle is higher. It is a ridge of rounded peaks rising abruptly from flatter surroundings. Its sands formed as shoreline ridges and dunes about two million years ago during the Pleistocene. The byway passes mainly along its eastern side. Cyclists use both the byway and other mountain roads for the challenge of terrain that is rugged compared with the surrounding area. Logging had stripped its hardwood vegetation by the 1920s; grapes, and later citrus, grew on its slopes.

moments.title: Montverde
moments.text: Montverde’s name came from a view across the water. A settler from Vermont arrived by boat on Lake Apopka and named the place Monte Verde, Spanish for green mountain, after its rolling hills. The community had earlier been called West Lake Apopka. It occupies the lake’s southwest shore. Montverde Academy became a central feature of the town after opening in 1912. The town incorporated in 1925, thirteen years after the school opened. The school began as Montverde Industrial School, then expanded in 1921 with a boys’ dormitory and a new dining hall.

moments.title: Winter Garden
moments.text: The West Orange Trail occupies the former railroad route down Plant Street’s median in downtown Winter Garden. The Orange Belt Railroad helped drive the town’s growth as citrus, turpentine and lumber production expanded. Stores gathered along Plant Street. Lake Apopka brought another trade: anglers came between the 1920s and 1960s, and the Edgewater Hotel opened to serve them. By the end of the 1960s, heavy lake pollution had collapsed that fishing industry. The trail approaches from Oakland over the rights-of-way of two neighboring lines, the Orange Belt Railway and the Tavares and Gulf Railroad.
